title: T1596.002 — Search Open Technical Databases - WHOIS
subtitle: Watch a fictional attack called Operation Paper Trail .
aria: Animated simulation of Operation Paper Trail. An attacker runs WHOIS and RDAP lookups against the Atlas Health Group domains, uses reverse WHOIS to find an old vendor portal and an expiring domain, waits for the domain to drop, registers it, and points its mail records at their own server. Defenders detect the takeover through brand monitoring and certificate transparency logs, then respond with a registrar dispute and a mailbox audit. A full written version follows below.

steps.caption: On a recon virtual machine, the attacker runs a WHOIS query for atlashealth.example . The request travels across the internet to the registrar WHOIS server on TCP port 43.
steps.defender: none - the query hit the registrar's server, not your network.

steps.title: The record comes back
steps.caption: The server answers with the public record: registrant organization Atlas Health Group , an admin email, the name servers, the creation date, and the expiry date. The attacker now knows who owns the domain and how it is hosted.
steps.defender: this data is public by design; minimize it with WHOIS privacy and role-based emails.

steps.title: Reverse WHOIS pivot
steps.caption: The attacker feeds the admin email into a reverse WHOIS service. It returns three related domains, including an old vendor portal that the company forgot about. One contact detail mapped the whole portfolio.
steps.defender: reverse WHOIS on your email leaks every domain that mentions it - use role-based registration emails.

steps.title: Expiry check finds a weak spot
steps.caption: The attacker checks dates on each related domain. One, grants.atlashealth.example , expires in 9 days. It has no auto-renew and no registrar lock. That is an open door.
steps.defender: registrar lock plus auto-renew removes this window entirely.

steps.title: Watch and wait; the domain drops
steps.caption: The attacker sets a watch on the domain and waits. Nobody renews it. The registration lapses and the name becomes available to anyone, anywhere, within seconds.
steps.defender: silence while the attacker waits - this is exactly why domain hygiene matters before the drop.

steps.title: Re-registration and mail hijack
steps.caption: The attacker registers the dropped domain through a fast registrar, points its MX records (the mail routing rules in DNS) at their own mail server, and puts up a clone of the old portal. Mail for that domain now flows to the attacker.
steps.defender: brand monitoring plus certificate transparency watching catch this within hours.

steps.title: Defenders see it
steps.caption: The SOC (Security Operations Center) brand monitor flags a new registration containing the company name. At the same time, a new TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificate for the domain appears in public Certificate Transparency logs. The SOC correlates the two alerts and sees the MX change.
steps.defender: correlate new registrations and new certificates for your brand strings into one case.

steps.title: Response
steps.caption: The team files an abuse report with the registrar, starts a UDRP dispute (the arbitration process for domain ownership), audits mailboxes for mail that was silently swallowed during the drop, and re-secures every other domain in the portfolio.
steps.defender: check mail logs for messages you may have missed during the drop window.
